title: How Do Big Ships Collide on Rivers? A Tanker Struck a Docked Riverboat in New Orleans
fb_caption: On Friday 13 November, a tanker struck a docked riverboat on the Mississippi River in New Orleans. The riverboat capsized at the dock, and officials said everyone on board was accounted for. Investigators say the tanker's steering failed about two minutes before impact, and the cause is still being investigated. So how do big ships end up hitting things on rivers? Three big reasons: huge momentum with no brakes, a narrow bending channel with a current that never stops, and almost no room when steering or power fails. Have you ever watched a giant ship squeeze past on a river? Tell us where below.

beats.text: On Friday, November thirteenth, a tanker struck a docked riverboat on the Mississippi River in New Orleans. The riverboat capsized at the dock. Officials said everyone on board was accounted for.

items: THE RIVERBOAT CAPSIZED AT THE DOCK

beats.text: Investigators say the tanker's steering failed about two minutes earlier, and they are still working out why. So how do big ships end up hitting things on rivers? Here are the three big reasons.

overlays.text:
HOW DO SHIPS COLLIDE
ON RIVERS?

beats.text: One: momentum. A big ship can weigh tens of thousands of tons, and it has no brakes. Even with the engine thrown into reverse, it can travel many times its own length before it stops.
Two: the river itself. The channel is narrow, it bends, and the current never stops pushing. Some river bends are so tight that ships have to take turns going through.

Three: no room for failure. A rudder only works when water flows past it, and steering needs power. Lose either one at sea and there is space to drift. On a river, the bank, a bridge or a dock can be seconds away.
It is like steering a loaded truck down an icy alley lined with parked cars.

So how is the risk kept low? Local river pilots guide the big ships. A Coast Guard traffic service watches the river around the clock, a bit like air traffic control. And tugs can be called in to help.

overlays.text: HOW THE RISK IS KEPT LOW

beats.text: Takeaway: on a river cruise or a ferry, treat the safety briefing like the one on a plane. Know where the life jackets are, and know your nearest way out.

items: TREAT IT LIKE A PLANE BRIEFING
KNOW WHERE THE LIFE JACKETS ARE
